blocks.x: Alright, let's go ahead. Do you want to give me a name first? Well, my right name is Minor Hall. And as far as this rhyme is concerned, Kid already gave me that nickname.
Oh, he did.

Yeah, he did. When I first started out, I was so fast to start the playing, even before he'd knock off a number. That's what we used to do in Yorling, you know, that stomp off. So, first he called me a round of go, because I was always ready. That's where the first of it started. That was back in New Orleans. Yeah, that was in Yorling's. When I first played with Oren, and how that happened was his drummer, a fellow by the name of Henry Martin, I don't remember him. I never knew him but he was. I used to go down to St. Catherine Hall where they played on Sunday night, and sat in one night, and I played so much like him. In other words, the rhythm. And so, his drummer laid off one night, and Oren had me to work in his place. And I played so well like him, so close to him, until Oren, until Oren hired me several times to play in his place when he couldn't make it. So, after that, my brother, Tubby Hall, he really gave me my face starting the playing. Now, who was the oldest? Tubby was. Tubby was older. Tubby was older. Yeah, yeah. He was two years older than me.
Well, I wonder, because they called him Baby Hall.

Yeah, that was his nickname, Baby. I thought he was the youngest in the family. No, no, they called him Baby. And one day I was fooling around on St. Yolens, we used to call them Steps, Front Steps, and Gary and all that stuff. So he gave me a pair of sticks one day. So I started to beat around on the porch and the steps and the way I could, and practically that's how I picked up drumming.
Well, when were you born? Do you remember your birthday?
I was born on 2nd of March, 1897, in a place called Sellers, Louisiana.
How's that spelled?
Sellers, that's about 18 miles out in Yolens. They're going north.
Going north. Up towards Baton Rouge. That's right. Which side of the river? Well, that was, well, let's see. Near Laplace, where Aure was born?
No, this is the other side of the river. See, I was right across from Hornsville.
Well, well, Monroe came from the other side over there, St. James Parish.

Yeah, that's right. I think Papa Mutt, too, came from Hornsville. Yeah, I grew up in Hornsville. Yeah, so after all my mother and father, they moved from Yolens, I think I was about two years old, and I was practically raised in Yolens, and my brother, I don't know how he got started. See, my father was a drummer. Oh, was that like a drummer? Yeah, my old man, he used to play in brass band and things up in the country. What was his name? His right name was Joseph Hall. Yeah, and he was a drummer.
Did he play up in the country or down in New York?

Yeah, in the country. No, he used to play in brass band. Up there, they had a brass band? Yeah, yeah, one of them in Yolens, Louisiana brass band. So I don't know how my brother started, but he gave me these sticks. So that's how I picked it up myself. So my first plane was, he used to work for Dennis, a Dr. Graw in New Orleans, and he used to go down below the city in Plaquemine Parish, I think you call it that, with a fellow by the name of Till. He used to hire the fellows out of New Orleans and go to play down in a place called Plaquemine Parish. Charlie Love and Clarence Williams came from there. Yeah, Zeb, Splendid Platt, they all came from down that way.

So one time, my brother couldn't get off. Well, excuse me, do you know Zeb's real name, his last name? No, all I knew was he's Zeb. No, I never could think of his last name, Clarence Platt. I believe Professor Minetta, who was here last night, said something like L-E-N-O-I-R.

Well it could be, but we always called him Zeb or Zeb. So he couldn't make the trip. And in the meantime, I still was wearing short pants. So my brother asked me, he said, do you think if I let you go to my place, could you make it? He said, well, I don't know, I'll try. So I had to borrow a pair of long pants to put on. So I went in his place, the fellow, his boy was, he played clarinet and guitar. His first name was Koyko. Oh yes. Yeah. He talked about the California years. Yeah, he died, you know. So I went in my brother's place, and I made good. So from then on he hired me, he wouldn't hire my brother no more.
Well do you remember, by the way, when Tubby was born, what year?
Well, let me see. He was, I was two years older than him, and I was born in 97, so I met him. He was born, I don't know what month, but that's your name, born in 95. 95.

Around 95, because I was two years older than him. I don't want to interrupt so much, but while we were talking about Tubby, what was his real name and how did he get that name? His right name was Fred Hall. Oh that's right, Fred.

Fred Hall, yeah. Now where he got this Tubby from, he got so fat. Oh yeah, he was fat when I was born. They quit calling him Babin, they called him Tubby, they used to call him Big Tubby, and they used to call me Little Tubby.
Little Tubby, I never heard that.

Oh yeah, they used to call me Little Tubby. So that's what started me to play him. So finally when I, the first band that I, it was a three piece band, a fellow by the name, Arthur Campbell, I'm a piano player, I don't know if you've ever heard of him. I've heard of him, yes. Arthur Campbell and Sidney Bechet.
Oh yeah.

And we had a three piece band down on Gidresson Alley, I mean the man around the place was Gidresson Alley, it was upstairs at the nightclub, and that's my first job with three pieces. So after I did so well, then my brother and Eddie Garland, Sugar John and a bunch of them, that's when they first went to Chicago.
Oh yeah.

Yeah, they went up there, and they had a band at the Deluxe Cafe. Lawrence Dewey with them. That's right, I think Lawrence Dewey had a band at that time, yeah. So he was up there working with them at the Deluxe Cafe at 35th and State, a fellow by the name of Shaw. And so about later on my oldest brother went up to Chicago, but he wasn't a musician. So that left my mother, my father, and myself still in New Orleans. So that's when he sent for the three of us. When I first went up to Chicago, I didn't have any job playing, but in the meantime my oldest brother was working at Stockyard, and he had charge of the laundry department or something there. So when I went up there, he told me to come out one morning to see about a job, which I did, and the job that they give me was in the spare room department, and all the floor was full of water. He had to walk in the water, and I didn't even have no boots. So I walked out the next fire escape and went home. So I didn't do anything. In the meantime, my brother got drafted in World War I. That's when I got my chance. I'd taken his place.
And you both went to Chicago the same trip, the same time?
No, no. The turbine went ahead of me.
Oh, when you said the three of you went, I didn't know.
No, my father and mother and myself. I see. They sent to the three of you.
Yes, I see. Your older brother sent to the three of you.
That's right.
Is your older brother already there?

Yeah, he went up with Tebberway. But he was a musician. So after I got around, I got introduced to some of the fellas around, and I played a few little jobs, and I can't think who it is now. But anyhow, when my brother got drafted, and him and my oldest brother went at the same time, and so that's why I'd taken his place.
You were too young to get them involved.

Yeah, I wasn't quite old enough yet for the first draft. So when he went, I'd taken over, and in the meantime, I don't know what happened to Tuley Garland, but when I wound up, Breaux was playing bass, Wilmer Breaux. So that wound up with Wilmer Breaux, Sugar Johnny, Lawrence Dewey, Roy Palmer, myself and Lil Hardin. See, she was then Hardin, it wasn't Armstrong's right there. There's a picture, I've seen that picture of that band. Yeah, that's right. So we made it so good up there, at the meantime, Sugar Johnny they called him, the trumpet player. Smith was his name. Smith, yeah. He's taken sick. He went into T.B. So he just blowed till he couldn't blow no more. So I can't tell just how the band got left the job, but anyhow, we went to work at the Dreamland for Bill Bottoms. So while we were working there, Oliver came to town with a show called Mary Mack.
Oh yeah.
Yeah. So when Sugar Johnny died.
I guess that was his girlfriend for a while.

Yeah. So after Sugar died, I think if I'm not mistaken, I don't know who was playing trumpet. Well anyhow, no that's right, they got in Mud Carey, that's right. Mud Carey came in there once. That's right. Mud Carey came in there. And Johnny Dodds came up there together. Yeah. I don't know how the mix up come up, but it was at the Dreamland, then the band changed a little. Papa Mud was playing trumpet and Dodds was playing clarinet then. So at the meantime, Papa Mud wanted to take a trip back to New Orleans. So Oliver came to town with a show and Mud talked with Oliver about working, could he come back and work two weeks in his place. So they arranged the thing and at the meantime, while Mud was gone, Oliver took the band over. That's how he got the band. So then after Oliver took the band over, we worked the Dreamland for a pretty good while, and then we had two jobs. See we used to go to work, at that time night club, she called it one o'clock. Then we went to work down to Pekin after hours. And Tony Jackson was playing intermission piano. At the Pekin, I think.
Yeah, at the Pekin.

So we worked down there a while, then after that we got out of there, there was so much trouble down there, we lose that job, we close the place up I think. Yeah, there's some shooting on there. Yeah, there's some gangsters there. Yeah, there's some gangsters, that's right. Because that's the first time I've ever seen Al Capone. Yeah, he used to come up there to gang all the time. So after that closed up, somehow Oliver got in touch with working over at Lincoln Garden, it was the Royal Garden there. See. So we had two jobs. We used to go from one place to the other, and so finally got to the place where, I don't know what happened, but anyhow, when we were working at the Dreamland at the time, Oray was up in, that time in Oakland.
Mm-hm.

So some man up there, I forget his name, he wanted a Dixland band to work at a place called Pekrola Dance Hall on Market Street. I have a picture of that. Yeah, so he got in touch with these guys, so we had to add another man to the band to make eight pieces. So he picked up a fellow by the name of Jones. Well, Davey Jones.
Davey Jones.

He's still here. He's a historian. Yeah, he lives here. He was playing saxophone there. So after he joined the band, and Oliver was taking his job to San Francisco, that's when we went to San Francisco and work up there. So after we started working there a while, I don't know, maybe the people didn't go for Dixland, so they would go to the dance hall like they did. So Oliver wanted to lay off one man. So we think he should lay off Jones instead of Jimmy Pala. So that's when the mix-up come up. So I told him, I said, well, I'll have to stick with Jim. I said, we'll all come up together, and I don't see why I should lay him off. So Oliver got kind of peeved about it. So he says, well, if you don't like it, you can go with him just like that. Well, he tried to say that I quit, but I didn't. So in the meantime, he gave me a notice, and so the union taken it up. So we had a case, and we had to go for the board about it. So when I wound up, they made him pay me all my expenses back home, and I think it made him pay me a month's work or something like that. And they found him around $150 for sending for Baby Dots. That's how Baby Dots got to play with him. See, he sent for Baby Dots without getting permission from the union. And if I'm not mistaken, I think they found him $300. So that's how I fell out with Oliver. So at the meantime, I went back to Chicago. And when I went back to Chicago, Jimmy Noon hired me. So at the meantime, Tegra was playing with Carl Dixon, the big band at Sunset across the street from where I was working. The place we were working at, I opened up with Jimmy Noon, Earl Hines, Joe Poston, and if I'm not mistaken, I think Johnny was playing, I'm not sure. Was that the drums? No, see. The drummer, I was trying to think. No, no, no. I mean you went in the 40th. We opened the place. You opened the whole.
At that time they called it the Ness.
Yeah. They changed the name after that. So we were working at the place. I was working at the place.
We were working at the place.
We were working at the place.
We were working at the place. And then they met out there.
So we went to work there. So I worked there while with Jimmy, Earl Hines. We had a good job.

So finally I had a little run in with a girl there, you know, working in a check room and come to find out she was married. So that broke that up. So she started disturbing. At the meantime, Ora set for me to come to Los Angeles to work at a Texas dance hall, because the drummer they had had two jobs.

He had opened up. No, here. In Los Angeles? Yes. He left Oakland and came down here. At that time, Texas dance was going on there. Well, I never knew. I thought you stayed out here on the coast. I never knew you were back in Chicago.

No, I went back in Chicago. Yes. So, pardon me, so after this mess come up, so I said I'd better take this job. Well, in the meantime, I bought my own ticket. He didn't have to send it for me. I wanted to get away from Chicago. So when I came back to Los Angeles, the drummer they had had given me his two weeks notice. Well, the lady was working for her, he went singing the blues to her, so she changed it, and she fired him. That'd take the whole band of some mess to the head. Well, anyhow, they voted on the thing. And when they voted on it, they beat me by one vote. They keep it. So at the meantime, I said, well, I'm out here, I'll stay. But Ory and them wanted to send me back. They said, no, I'll stay out. So what Ory and Papa Mutt named there, first Ory said he quit. So that's why when Ory left the job, and Mutt left, then we made up to sell the band, and we went to work down at St. Peter over. And at the meantime, I worked down there, well, I just stayed out here, and I've been working with Ory since. I can't think what year it was in.
That Taxi Dance Hall, was that on 3rd Street?

Yeah, 3rd, right off of Maine. There was two we worked. We worked one there and one at a fellow by the name of Jack Goldboy. See, he had one. It's called Red Mill. So we worked this Taxi Dance Hall until Ory got lined up pretty good, and that's when we changed the band a little around. Then we had the real band we had. We had Bud Scott, Papa Mutt, Eddie Garland, myself, Ory, and I think we had Fred Washington for a while.
We saw Fred Washington last night.

Yeah, for a while, but I don't know, and I would change it on, so that's when Ory started to do a nightclub work, and he went over so big, so people just was crazy about him out here. And so I've been with Ory ever since, up to 1957. Now I think, I can't think what year that was, but it was pretty old back, you know, a long time ago.
In the 1928s? Something like that.

Cure or so. Yeah, because, and then after that, when things got, just before the war I think it was, things got pretty bad around there for music. Yeah, I remember that. Yeah. So. Or he had a chicken farm and all that. And Papa Mutt, I think he went to work on a road, Porter, and I went to work at a place they call it Strip City now. It's a bird on Peacorn Western with a five piece band. A fellow by the name of Winner Island had it. And then that's where I got drafted again.
Yeah, drafted in two R's. In two R's.
Yeah, I got drafted there. How old were you then? 44 years old.
44 years old.
Yeah. I got drafted again.
Were you married then?

No, I was single. Because the guys was kidding. They said Uncle Sam got it in for you. He said you must have been a good soldier in World War I. So I got drafted again, and that's why I went back in service again. And I went up to Fresno, California when I got stationed there. So I didn't move, I stayed up there about a year. And at the meantime, at my age, the men could get out, but they had to take a defense job.
Oh yeah, I remember that.

And as far as the government was concerned, they still had to hold it. So I wrote in for an application for Douglas, at the Center of Monica, and I received it and through there they sent me over there. And I worked for Douglas two years, up until just before the war ended, in the meantime, I made up a band out of the plant. I had two girls and a six piece band and everybody said, what the devil are you doing here? Like you can play. And I said, well the government still got a hold of him. Well we used to let us play on Wednesdays and Fridays, an hour, you know, for the people while they eat. So one day, as the war was getting to an end, there was another fellow who had a choice to entertain them. A fellow was a wrestler, and the fellow was a different department than I was in, where the guy just liked me. So he came to me one day, he says, Hall, you fellas can get out of here now. I thought he was kidding me. I said, is that really true? He says, yeah. So one day I went out, it was, or at the meantime, I think Bonnie somebody talked over to going the plane again. Yeah, he was with Bonnie. He was with Bonnie. Yeah. So I made up the van again, and the night they got a job at a place called a jade. Yeah, I remember what that was on time. On Hollywood Boulevard. Yeah. So in the meantime I said, well I think I can make it, but I've got to go out to the plant. I said, I don't have to go. You don't have to go. The day I went out that afternoon at four o'clock, that's the same night we were supposed to open the jade. So I went out there with a tuxedo and thing on, and go from there to go to work, to turn in my badge and thing. And when I walked up to the gate with my badge on, everybody started to whistling at me, you know what I'm saying. You're not working in a tuxedo and thing like that, are you? I said, no, I'm quitting. So at the meantime I looked around and found my supervisor, and went in the office with him, and he said, what gives here? I don't get all this tuxedo business. I told him, I'm leaving. He said, you can't do that. I said, yeah, I'm leaving. I'm sorry, I've got to leave. So I'm quitting. So he talked to me about a half hour, and time was getting close for that to be in Hollywood. So he talked to me about a half hour, and he said, well, Hall, you're a good worker, we'll give you another raise, and you've got a lifetime job if you want it. I said, no, I'm just going to leave. Well, he said, what you going to do? I said, I'm going back in the service. I didn't want to tell him I was going back to play music, because I wasn't sure yet. So he said, well, you still just got out of it, didn't you? I said, no, I'm going back there. He said, I can cook. I'm going back in the Merchant Marine. So I said, you see, he couldn't do no good. He signed these papers and things, and he shook hands with me, and I broke my neck out of there to get back to Hollywood, because it was seven o'clock then, and I had to be out there at eight o'clock. So that's when I opened up in the jail. So the first week I worked, and the second week, my supervisor come in there with some people following the thing, and they seen me, and he says, thought you was going back in the Merchant Marine. I said, well, they said I was a little too old. So I just went on back to play music, so they just skipped it at that. So that's when we worked in the jail as long as we did, and from then on, we just nightclub right on through.
Yeah. When Ory first got his band together working for those radio arson wells, you know, they had Zutty. Yeah, that's right. You were in the factory then.
I was in the factory, and I couldn't get out there. I wondered why you were working with Ory. No, when I picked up that, when he was working for the Standard Oil Company.
That's where I got to know.

That's when I got to see Zutty. After he hired Zutty, well, they had quite a little trouble with Zutty and all. He was an all right fellow, but just see Ory was a peculiar fellow by the time. He used to rush the temper.
Yeah, that's what they say.

He was a good drummer, but that was his biggest fault. And he's always had a squad with the piano players all the time. He wanted to play like he, his temper. So that's why him and Ory practically fell out. It wasn't his playing, it just, that was his trouble. So that's, I got back in the pits again, and I've been with Ory since then, Z.

I was going to ask a little bit more about your very first days, those bands up in the country. How old were you when you moved into New Orleans? I was about two and a half years old. Oh, very. You didn't remember anything. Oh no, nothing out then.

No, I was too young for that. The only thing first I can remember about music in New Orleans was when I was big enough to play and learn how to play, my biggest admirers, three things I wanted to do was to play a funeral, a mardi gras parade, and something else I can remember. I said if I'd ever do that I'd be satisfied. No, play it for a picnic. For a picnic.
Like that?
Go up on a boat. See, they used to have excursion boats, and go up the country, and play that. And Ory used to get a lot of that stuff. Oh yeah. Right on the Mississippi River.
Yeah.
So I practically take the guy's job away from him. Yeah. They overhired me right on. I don't know why.

Henry Martin. Yeah. I asked Ory last week, we saw him a week ago today, this time about, we were up there until six o'clock, and I said how come, well we were asking about something else, for a while he was going to use little Joe Lindsey on drums.
Well Joe did play with him a while.

And I said how come you used him, I thought Henry Martin was your drummer. He said well, something funny, like he said Henry Martin wanted to take up guitar, he said he played guitar and dropped his drums for a while, something like that.
So I guess that's it. He did use, he used Johnny Lindsey, I think it was.
Joe. Joe Lindsey. Johnny was the bass player.

Yeah, Johnny Lindsey. Yeah. I'll tell the truth but I don't know him much. You never knew? No, no. See I left there, see I left New Orleans in 1918. 1918 is when you went to show up. Yeah, so I don't know much about those stuff at all. I didn't even know George Rush till I met him on here. No, that's right. He was younger, he came up later. No, I didn't know anything about him. He didn't come up until 1920s. I think he had a little fella, I think what you call him, he played piano with him a while, Steve Lewis. He'd been with Piron a lot too.
Yeah, they always talked about Steve Lewis and this Johnny you talking about, the drummer
here. So I don't know anything about him, you know, like that. I was going to ask a little bit more about Tubby, I always call him, I didn't know your

brother so well but I've heard him play with Johnny Dodds. Everybody called him Tubby. So I always think of him just as Tubby, you know. He played with Nanny Dominick, you remember Nanny? Yeah, they came out here, I was living out here then, and he came out with a show, I think it was called the Charleston Review. I didn't know him. Yeah, they came out and was playing with Nanny Dominick, you remember Nanny?

Yeah, they came out here, I was living out here then, and he came out with a show, I think it was called the Charleston Review. I didn't know him. Yeah, they came out and was playing with Nanny Dominick was playing, and oh they had a pretty
good sized band.

They played at the Pan Amish Theater then, they had a stage show then. And that's when I seen my brother, and I told him I wanted to go back home, and he sent me back. And I came right on back there again, I made four trips, three trips, and the fourth trip I stayed.
Stayed out?

Stayed out. No, it was in September, and it was getting too cold, I said I'm going back to California, and I've been living here ever since. But he, as far as Tubby's concerned, a lot of people thought we'd play, it was a little different than our playing. He kept, he had a different rhythm, a little different.
Well Baby Dodds said that he had a famous press roll, that Baby copied his press roll from Tubby.

Yeah, a good right foot. Good foot too. Yeah, yeah, that guy, his pedal was bent, I don't know whether the weight he put on it or what. That guy could play a show with his foot. I imagine that was that fast, see. But he was just a little different from us. See, Ori, that's one thing about I give Ori credit for him, he always liked good rhythm. He didn't want all that fancy stuff in there, but he wanted good rhythm. And that's why I think I got a lot of credit from what he taught me, you know. I give him that credit. He really put me on the ball when it comes down to that.
What kind of a drum set did you have when you started out? Your very first drum set? Or what you played on Tubby's set I guess when you started.

Yeah, the first one he gave me, that time I had a wooden drum. I had a snare drum, pretty good size, I forget how big it was. And all kind of a make up set, you know. One cymbal and one cowbell. And at that days they wasn't used a hi-hat cymbal then. The cymbal was on the side of the drum, yeah, see. Worked with the foot pedal. That's right, together, yeah. And a pair of sticks, that's all. Nothing there. Did you have any wood blocks? Yeah, any wood block. But I mean, as anything else, nothing else. Nothing at all. Just two drums, pair of sticks, and a cowbell and a wood block.
How big was your bass drum?
Oh, in them days it was, well the one, I used a 24. They looked like around 20 to 29, big case of them, yeah. Most of them were 28.
One time they had one where you'd tighten those ropes.
Oh yeah, you'd pull those sticks.
Yeah, you'd pull them, yeah, wet them, you know.

Pull them with that, that's right. And we had gut sneds on them there. See, we didn't have wire sneds like that. I had an old time set on there. What was your first foot pedal like? It was, the pedal was made out of wood, like a hinge, you know.
Yeah.

And then the rod go straight up, and the spring was on top of it. See, you hook it. Oh yeah. Yeah, and the ball was in the middle, and you hit it that way. See, the spring pull it on top. See, the rod go straight up through that head. I forget what pedal they called that. No, it wasn't like pedal they got nothing. It wasn't homemade though. Oh no, they buy them that way. Yeah, they buy them that way. They buy them that way. They were a rod go over your drum. Yeah. And then you hook it on the back, the thing that you screw your, like you tighten your drum with, you know, the thing you had and the clamps of that, and it had a strap, you know, and you swing that way. Oh yeah, different kinds of pedal, that's what you're using there.
Did they respond pretty quickly? Yeah, they were right.
They were fast. Sure, just as fast as the one they got now. Sure they were. Very good pedal. Very good pedal. Yeah, very good.
Who were the, of course you liked your brother's drumming, I know that, because he was a little older and you knew him better. Yeah. But the other drummers, the early drummers, who did you hear?
and who did you like?

Well, my favorite drummer was Chick Webb. Well, Chick Webb. That was my favorite drummer. You didn't hear him until late years. Until late years, but I mean, he was my favorite drummer of all time. He wasn't fancy or nothing like that.

He was just a good drummer and a good cymbal maker. Yeah, he was really good. Then I liked Peggy, something hard. He used to play with the Tennessee 10th. I never knew. No, he was a good drummer. But my favorite drummer after I was big enough and got into the music game was Chick Webb. That was my favorite drummer.

Did you hear him out here or was it in New York? No, I heard him in Chicago once. Well, he was in Chicago. Once, yeah. I think it was one of the show when I did. Yeah. I heard him at the Apollo Opera in the Harlem Opera House in 125th Street. Yeah, well, he was my favorite drummer. Savoy Ballroom. I didn't know he got out west anyway because he was crippled and didn't know how much. No, this was Chicago.
I heard him. What's your call? Yeah. No, I never seen him. I think he's been out here. Yeah, he played. Yeah, but I've never heard him out at all.
Of the New Orleans drummers, do you remember any of the early ones like old man Contrell or Contrell?
Yeah, yeah.
I remember him.
He was mostly, he used to play at the Lyric Theater all the time.
Oh, the John Robeshow? Yeah. And the band.
That's right, yeah. Him and, well, the drummers in the Orleans in those days, I did like Henry Zeno.
Oh, yeah?
Yeah. He was a pretty fast drummer in those days.
Remember which band he played with? Henry? He mostly worked nightclubs.
You know, the clubs down next to when the district was over.
More than the district.
Yeah, that's right. That's my first band, Henry Zeno. Well, I guess he worked with Oliver there.
Yeah, he did.
Quite a while.
I'd known he worked uptown, I think, with the Eagle Band, Frankie Doosen up at St. Mastonic Hall. I didn't know if you heard him up there.
Yeah, I've heard him.
Where did you live when you went to New Orleans then?
I used to live 4431 Forest Street. Up in Theretway? Yeah, that's between Napoleon Avenue and Jennings.
Yeah, that's on the way up to Tulane University. There's not four of them up there. Yeah, we'd go by there every time we'd. That's right.

That's where I used to live. That's where I used to live. The number was what, 40? 4431 Forest Street. 4431. Yeah, my cousin owned a place, Old Man and the Umpers. I don't know if you've heard of him. Oh, Jim. Jim, Old Jim Umpers. Old Jim, the old man that taught music. That's right. He owned...
He was your uncle?
No, his cousin. Your cousin? Yeah, his son used to play clandest. Yeah, Willie. Pop-up. No, no, old man. See, Willie was... Uh...
Umphreys. The Percy Umpers plays coronet now as the leader of the Eureka Band. Oh, is it? Yeah, sure. We first cousins.

First cousins. Yeah. And the old man, you know, he used to have... In those days, he'd call them dump carts, you know, it's the whole dirt and thing. Yeah. See? Yeah, we first cousins. Because I was surprised to hear about Earl playing trombone, you know.
Yeah, he's over in Virginia now, plays bass. Oh, do he? Plays bass.
Yeah, I know he was playing trombone at the time. Yeah, he did for many years. And Percy, I don't know, he was playing drums too, I heard.
Yeah, Percy started on drums. Drums, yeah.

And then he's now a cornet. He hasn't played drums for years. Is that so? Mm-hmm. So I had never heard him, you know. Willie, I played with Willie. Willie came out here and we were working someplace and he worked a week or two somewhere out here. We were using two clarinets. I think he got out to Navy out here or something. And that's the first time I heard him play. But he went on back to New Orleans.
Yeah. Any other drummers you can remember there? Ever hear of Walter Brundy? Yeah, sure. How was he? He was a good drummer.

See, another day that I remember, Walter Brundy and the Zeno, while old man Contrell and now let's see, I can remember. Old timers. No, that's... Remember Mac Murray? No, I don't, no. I've heard of him, but I don't remember him.
Or Chandler, D.D. Chandler.
Yeah, no, I don't remember those guys. Ever before your time? Yeah, they were for mine, because the first time I ever heard Buddy Bowling play, I was a youngster. I went out to Lincoln Park.
Oh, yeah?

I heard him play once. Seen him once. But I never, I mean, come in contact or play with him, nothing like that. Because I didn't do much playing around. All the band I played around in the Orleans was over at the time, and the little band I went down to Cuts and played with, and this job I had was Sidney Bichon off the camel.
Oh, yeah?
We had a three-piece band. But I don't remember much of the guys, because I left there, you know, 1918 and all.
Can you remember Sidney about the same age as you? Sidney Bichon?
Mm-hmm.
He was about three, four months different than our age. Just a few months. He told me he was born in 97. Yeah, that's right. And Baby Dodds once said he thought he was a little older. No.
What I mean, that's a close eye.
Yeah, not three or four years. No, no.
Just a few months. I looked a record of what we had by this age. It was about two, three months different.
Months different.

He looks older, you know, in years, but no. No, basically he's about the same age. All different, about two, three months different. Yeah. Because when I was in Europe in 57, to me, basically it looked like he was a lot older than what
he is. Yeah, he does.

Yeah, a lot older, see. But no, he basically is not that old, see. Because the first time, it's like Louis, the first time I seen Louis in a parade when he was in that Holmes. But I didn't see him until he came to Chicago to John Oliver's band, see. And that's the first time I seen Louis in a parade. Yeah.
I was wondering about if you ever did hear any brass band up in the country like your father's I was too young. Even in late years, if you went up for a visit.

No, no. No. Never did hear. Never did go back. No. The only band when I got larger was I used to listen to, I think one of them was the Seltzer Brass Band. Yeah. And the Tuxedo Brass Band, I think Papa Seltzer's band had that. Yeah, he had that. But no Mardi Gras Day, well they'd make up a lot of bands, you know, they'd just pick up guys, because I know a lot of guys would just can of horn, fill out the band. Yeah, no Mardi Gras Day. And I played several Mardi Gras parades, and that was the biggest thing in the funerals. I played a few funerals.
Was it, you didn't belong to any organized band then at all in the brass band regularly? No, no regular brass band.
Did you play snare or bass drum? Snare drum.
Ever played with your brother in a parade down there?
No, never have.
Never worked with my brother in anything.

Never worked with them again? Never had, no. The only time, the closest I come around my brother playing, when I was living out here, I went back to Chicago. The Elf Convention in Chicago and the Elf had a brass band here, and Papa Mudd at the time had an eight piece band out here, and they hired this band to play for their balls on the way back. See we played one in San Francisco, one in Oakland, one in Denver, Salt Lake, and St. Louis in Chicago. In the meantime we were hired to play with the brass band in the parade. So I played, I beat snare drum in the parade, the head down on the stand was two snare drums. And when we got to Chicago I played, you know, with the band that way. And we played for the Elf's Convention in Chicago. I forget the year we did, but it was a very long time ago.

I was going to ask too about any regular formal lessons, if you, when you learned to play drums, did your brother show you how to hold the sticks a little bit, or did you ever have a book that you learned in? No, he showed me how to hold the sticks.
The first time I ever learned how to read a note was there on Chicago. Jimmy, a fellow by the name of Jimmy Burtrain.
Oh yeah, Jimmy.
Jimmy was playing that time, if I'm not mistaken, at the theater at 35th and State, I forget the name of it.

It was one grand theater. It was a grand theater, that was at 31st. I think it was the State Theater. It was a monogram. Yeah, it was a monogram, and it was the State Theater. The State, that's right. That's right.

What's going to have the band in there? Ed Bailey. Oh, I never knew. Yeah, well, he lives here now, he works at the post office. Ed Bailey, because he had the band in World War I, in the 8th Regiment. Well, I met Jimmy, he was crazy the way I played rhythm. He said if I show him how to do it, he learned me how to read. That's the first time I ever read a note. He gave me my first lessons of how to read, which I'm not a great reader now, but he gave me my idea of it. But all through New Orleans, I couldn't read a note. Just played anything out of my ear. Yeah, couldn't read a note.
Jimmy Burtrain played xylophone too, didn't he? Oh, he's a good drummer.
He didn't teach you anything like that. No, no, he was just a few things to read enough for me to get by with.
Did your brother ever learn to read? Yeah.
Do you know? Yeah, yeah. Yeah, he's taking lessons, but from who I don't know. Yeah, he could read pretty good. Yeah?

Yeah. Now, when did he go to, I don't want to keep harping on your brother, but since he isn't here to tell himself about his life, and I never did talk to him very much, there's so little known about him that you would be the one who could explain better. Do you remember just when he went to Chicago? You say he went before you did. I think he went to Chicago in the latter part of 1917.
He was gone about three, four months before I went up, so I went in 1918.
I had the idea that I talked to him once and it seemed like he'd told me maybe as early as 1915, but not that early. No, I think he went in 1917.
Not 17.
He went up before Oliver did.
Oh yeah, oh yeah, I even went before Oliver did. That's right, you were up there. Or any of this. That's why I met him. I only came to go to the band.
Did Tubby go up there to play then too, on drums, on another job? It seems...
No, I think he went to Chicago, but I don't know how he got into the deluxe cafe business, but he joined the band up there. He didn't leave with them.
That's what I thought.

No, no, no, because they went, I think Garland said he went up there in 1912, but it was later than that. See? No, he went up after them, and how he got into this band I don't know, but he started playing with them. No, he didn't go up exactly, I don't know whether he was going to play music or what, but he just went to Chicago.

Seems to me like he told me that too, that he didn't go up there as a musician? No, he just went up there. Did he have any other trade, like for instance Manuel Perez and George Spiel and Dominic was a cigar maker?

No, no, no, he didn't, because most of what he did, he used to work in the office. He didn't have any other trade, like cigar makers or anything? No, no, he didn't, no. See, most of all the fellas were called a Creole guy.
They were downtown.
They did all that cigar making business and that. No, he used to work in the office for Dennis.
Homer Simeon, the same way, his father went up as a cigar maker.
Yeah, most of all those Creole fellas, they went up there and made cigar and things like that.
Did you ever learn any Creole language? A little.
See, on my father's side was Creole. Was that right? Yeah, not on my mother's side, whatever they call it, you know, see. No, I never could, I could speak a little, but I forgot anything.

Well, I guess you weren't any relation to the Halls that played clarinet like Edmund Hall and his brother Clarence. No, no, no, no relation at all. No relation? There's another fellow, Rene Hall, from there. No, no, no, no. No relation to him. No, anything to do with it.

Thought he'd clear that up, you know, because sometimes they'd make a mistake. Sure, no, a lot of people thought Edmund Hall and I were brothers. Yeah. No relation at all. First time I met him out here. Yeah. So there was no relation at all there, just a different Hall altogether. But when he went up the first time he didn't exactly go to play music, because see when he first went there, he first played with a fellow, he called him Dr. something, he used to play all the little forward and things around there. I can't think of his name. Now he was working with those bands before he joined Dixeland Band again. Yeah, he was doing all right.
Another thing, I've seen somebody told me that your brother might have gone up with Tigg Chambers. Do you remember Tigg Chambers ever?

Well, they went up too. They had a band, Tick Chambers, let's see what they had, but they came up after. No one else. No, they came up after that, see. Because all together at one time there was three bands up there from the all-in. Tigg Chambers, Ernest Kelly was playing a trombone I think. I've heard the name of it.
Yeah.
And then another band came back through there, was trumpet played by the name of, what was he, he was a Creole fellow. They had a band because they worked their while too.
Freddie Keffert of course. Well Freddie had been before, she was a show.

They were really the first drill band that went off. But at that time Dixieland wasn't going big. You see, when Dixieland started going big, in the meantime I was in New Orleans, believe it or not, I used to work for Lerocka's uncle. He had a grocery store at the corner of my house.
Well they had the original Dixieland? That's right.

Nick Lerocka. I went a couple of times with them. Then they went to New York, that's when they made the Liberty Stable Blues. You worked with that band? Yeah, I played them a couple of times around there, you know. They didn't think I could play, you know. And that's when they made up their band. They went to New York and made the Liberty Stable Blues and then things busted loose. And that was really telling the truth about it. They wasn't causing Dixieland really getting on top of it like they did. Yeah, they made it popular.
They sure did, they sure did. Yeah, they did. They made these records.
And then Freddie Kepler and them, they had a band all right, but people wasn't paying much attention to Dixieland.
Now I mean, and Yarlene was there because everybody played that one, but I mean after that, they
think this busted loose. stuff
Speaking of records, were you on that first date with Kid Ory, those Sunshine records for the Spikes Brothers?
No, no, no, Alton Redd. Boy out here, I'll call Alton Redd.
But I mean way back in 1921.

The first record I made was for Good Time Jazz. You never made those real old ones then? No, I think the first one I made was for Decker. The one you're talking about, they made them for Spikes Brothers.
Yeah, some real old ones, Dink Johnson. Yeah, no, I wasn't on that, no. Martin, Oliver, that's right.

Fred Horshyn can play piano. No, I was there. Alton Redd made them. And Alton Redd made them for Dr. Exner. I was in the Army then, I think, when they made them. Yeah, you were still in the Army. But the first record I made was from Nama State, Decker. Yeah, and that was good. Then Columbia. Then from then on, all the records I made was for Good Time Jazz.
Yeah.

Yeah. No, I wasn't on those records at all. Yeah, I wanted it out then. No, never did it first. The only records I ever made was then was we made some for Columbia and Decker. Then Orysine with Good Time Jazz.

At that time, that very first one, 1921, Dink Johnson played clarinetti. That's right, yeah. He played little drums. He'd been with Freddie Keppard and his brother Bill. Did you ever play with Dink? A few, like little one nights, you know. When he played piano then, I guess?
Yeah, yeah. Because I played once with him at Son of Barber. He lived up there.
He lived up there. I knew Dink very well when he had a place up by the ballpark, you know. That's right. Yeah, by the ballpark.

I made some records with him. Yeah, yeah. But I just, just gigs we called. Yeah. No, I never played. All the work, most I played out here with, was between Mutt and Ory. Well, practically Ory. At the time, I was working with this band in the war with Winslow Allen. Over the place they call it Strip City now. Peacorn Western. We were working at nightclub. That's why I got drafted in Army again.

I was going to ask a little bit about Mutt, since Mutt, Kerry, isn't here anymore. He did a talk for himself. In the first place, I was wondering about how old Mutt was. Do you think he was as old as Ory? Ory thought he was about the same age, maybe.

Well, I don't know. From my cousin, she told me Mutt is not as old as Ory. Wasn't as old. No, they may be about a year, two years different than the age. But he said he wasn't, but there's a big argument going on now about how old Ory is.
Yeah, that's right.

The paper said 71. No, he's older than that, because the reason I know he's older than that, we had a blowout for him in San Francisco. That's been about two years, three years since he was up there. And he made 71 then. So I think Ory is right there. He's around about 73 years old.
Yeah.
He was a right age, see.
Yeah.

He's about 73 years old. And Mutt was, I'd say about two years, wasn't much a year or two between. I'd always thought he was younger, too. No, no, no, because my cousin knows more, see, because she's about 65 now. She knows more, you know. And she said, no, Ory is, he's been sticking on that 71 for the last two, three years. Ory is about 73 years old.
I was going to ask him more about Mutt. When did you first play with him in Chicago, or did you play with him with Ory and New Orleans? In New Orleans.

Oh, yeah. Because I thought he was the greatest drummer in the world. Yeah. Because one time, when we used to play on the wagons, you know what I mean? We met King Oliver once, and hooked up, you know, on the bands, hooked up down there. And I'll never forget, he was playing his number of Simmons for Wobble.
Oh, yeah.
And he went to blow so high and he missed the note. And Ory at that time, Ory used to beat all the bands in the street.
For the hair. Oh, yeah. It wasn't so much, the way he played.

See, Ory used to play swing like that. He didn't play all them fast numbers there. It's just a certain rhythm, swing he had, and everybody went crazy about it. That's where he'd be. Sometimes a guy said, look out, Ory's in the street today. It's the guy with ducking, because, you know, people would get around and hoop and holler and they didn't want that. But Ory just had that rhythm swing, the people just went for it. And Ory had a good band, too. Oh, yeah. A tough band, but just the way Ory played, that swing, the way he did, that's how he beat
all the bands. That's how he beat them. I was going to ask about that boat, like the picnic that you said you went up the river.
Yeah, well, what we do was, say the picnic might be about some little town, you know, like Hornsville or somewhere. But we play on the boat going up.
For dancing, too, on the boat.

Yeah, on the boat. Have it be a colored boat ride. Yeah, yeah. A colored boat ride. Then they get off the boat, well, it's a picnic. We play for that. But coming back, it's all over. We don't play at all coming back.
That's right.
Everybody's sleeping.
Oh, wow. Yeah, they come down and swing fast under the boat. Yeah, that's right. That's right.

But I used to get a big kick out of that, playing on the boat. All it was big time was going up there, and wherever the picnic ground was, we play for that. And then another thing I got the biggest kick out of is playing out to the lake. I used to like to do that. Mellonburg. Mellonburg, West End, anywhere you had these picnets. Sometimes there'd be three or four bands out there. The guys blew it one of them. Just get a kick out of that. That was a great thing to do there.
I was going to ask about any of the church music you might have heard, and if you belonged to any church when you were in New Orleans.
Well, I used to go to Baptist church, you know. But since I came from California, I turned Catholic.
Most of the people downtown, they were Catholics. Oh, yeah, oh, yeah. I wonder if you were uptown if you were Baptist.

No, the biggest majority, well, the biggest majority of people in y'all was Catholic. That's right. That's all over, I guess. Oh, yeah, the biggest majority of people. I'd say nine percent of people. I suppose. And y'all needs to be Catholic, especially all drill people. Yeah, that's right. They were all Catholic.
Had you heard much music when you were a child in the churches?
No, not so much. Organs and things like that, you know. When I'd go, when we were kids, we had to go to Sunday school, see.
Because I remember Bud Scott and I think Mutt, too, had told us when they were children that there was good music that had that good beat in the churches.
Yeah, they kept a very good beat even in the churches.
No, they even told me that they thought Bolden got his idea of this whole jazz music from hearing those churches.

Well, I couldn't see, because I was too young. I didn't know anything about Bolden. I think when I first seen him, I was about twelve, fifteen years old. We kids used to walk out there, you know, just walk on over town. Because even when we started playing drums, you know, you would let us get on the street car.
That's right.
We had to walk. I see time I walked from the fairground to my house. Well, that's great.
That's a long way. Didn't think nothing of it.

No. See? Yeah. I'd walk from Carver City here one night just to be walking. But down there you had to carry drums. Now Eddie Garland, he had a pretty good system because he used to drive a barrel wagon. He'd pick up barrels. Now if he's going to play somewhere, he'd pick up his bass and take it in the wagon, see? But he had to walk back with it, see? The middle of the nights him and I, I'd walk, he'd play with Pop Foss and walk with it on his back and walk. That long walk would think nothing of it. Think nothing of it.
Well, I was going to ask a little bit about Bud Scott and since he isn't here too, just in general that old rhythm section of yours is about the best I ever heard.
Yeah, well see I first met Bud out here. I didn't know Bud Scott.
He didn't know him. He played the Robichaux down there. That's right.
I met Bud out here, Bud John O'Reilly's band. And at one time, I wouldn't brag about it, but I think we had one of the best. We had Bud Scott, Buster Wilson, Eddie Gawne and myself.
It was a wonderful, that's the best good in the next night I've ever heard from the person.
Yeah, I don't think he could beat it. No? He could beat it back, but he couldn't beat it.
Yeah.

And that's what O'Reilly made his reputation on. It wasn't so much playing, it was just that rhythm. Yeah, that was wonderful. The people out there just went crazy about it. They couldn't understand how we'd play like that. And O'Reilly used to play so soft. And that was loud.
That's right. I heard him playing so soft. It was real loud.
I might blast maybe the last chorus, the rockin' they call it rockin', but sometimes we played so soft you'd hear people dance on the floor.
Yeah.

Even in the late years I was hearing that. Oh yeah. I don't know how he's doing now, since you see O'Reilly, he's very particular about his band, and up to the last I was with him, he's very particular. He likes good rhythm, and he likes the band to shout all the time. So I don't know, I've heard several people say since they had no trouble now that sometimes you might get a drummer that don't suit in. Yeah, I think so. And I heard the last thing, they tell me he had a pretty good drummer, but he wasn't exactly a good pixel and drummer.
He was a good drummer.

The guy was good, I don't know who he was, now he had a good bass player, but he played a late modern bass, you know. And we had two and all, and we just stuck to that, and that's what the people out there weren't crazy about. They didn't care about playing no modern thing like that. They want us to play that same old style. That's why I say I'm sorry today, at his age, I think if he still had his band together, he'd still be going big.

Well I might ask you a little bit about your drums, like in playing two beat or four beat, did you ever change your style? That is in the old days as you maybe played two beat and then later four? Well that's a car to mostly with four beats.

See I was asked that question up in a station up in Oakland. Somebody brought up about four beats and two beats. I said, shoot, we'd been playing four beats when I was a kid playing. Even on the slow we used to play shorter than that, we'd play four beats. Sometime we'd play maybe two beats. But with that ain't nothing new.
No.
We'd always play four beats. See who started this two beats, there was what's called the band of the San Francisco blood or all that stuff. Blue Waters. Blue Waters, yeah. They played it.
Makes it sound like a heavy rhythm.

It really sounded like a brass band. They had an awful good band, but it sounded to me like a young brass band. Yeah, it didn't swing and that light drive. No, no, we played, O'er used to play even the blues, see, when he played that four beats. We used to call it rockin' time. Yeah, rockin' time. That's right. Because he always said he'd make people pass their foot, that's what we'd get it. But no, that's two beats, that just started years, you know, late years, people moth and that same, but we played four beats just like I had a fellow come out to the nightclub one night and he'd be a big studio drummer, and he couldn't understand how my drum was so sharp. He said he'd give anything in the world if he'd give his drum that sharp. I said well I can tell you I'd keep mine that way, I don't know if he can fix it that way. I said an old drummer, he taught me that his name was Cantrell. He said when you tighten your drum up, don't let it down. Just keep it up. Keep it up when you gotta move it. And sure might have sent my snares on it.
See. How thick a shell do you use? A five or six inch or how big is it? Do you know? Is it a fairly deep one or is it shallow?
I don't remember. The drum that I have now? Yeah. Oh no, it's about a... Here's a picture. Yeah, that's one of the drums I have. No. Is that the tom-tom? No, that's a drum.
That's a snare.
Oh yeah, sure, that.
Looks like about a six and a half or something like that.

Yeah, I used to use a big one. But that went out of the same time. I used to use them that big. Big as the tom-tom. Oh yeah, like on parades. Yeah. That's right. But no, it's a way of tuning a drum. Now I've had guys use my bass drum. You see, I tune my bass drum up.
Well, Baby Dodds told me he always does tune my bass drum up. Oh yeah, right these fellas like them soft down, you know.
I don't know. I tune, I've even tuned them out up to 10. A certain key on the key on the key. Yeah, that's a big one.
I think you said he was. Sure. Yeah, tune them up. One of them to B and one to A or one to E or something. A certain pitch.

Like I said about the studio drummer, I told him what to do and he came back the next week and said, it's fine now. Yeah. He loved the way I told him. I said old man Contra, taught me how to, he said all the way to let your drum down unless the weather gets too tight. But he said when you're tight, keep it up all the time. Don't let it down, because no matter what you do you can get it back in the same place again. So that's why my drums sound so good. And so far everybody that came out of the club, I would play it on my drums, said, how do you keep your drums this way? I said I don't like them. I had one boy play one night, and he turned mine down. He wanted that blabber sound like, I call it battle sound. No, no I don't tune, I keep mine up. It has nice sharp sound.

That's right, that's right. When did you start using the hi-hat or sock cymbal, what do you call that hi-hat or sock cymbal? That's a hi-hat cymbal. I thought well I got modern just like everybody else did, you know.

In the late years you know I had to follow a style too. That's what I said the other night when you hear, I'm doing a lot of things twenty years ago I don't think I had to do it. But I have to keep up, because if I had to stay like I was I never got no job. No, I've changed a little myself, but I still try to keep that. Same beat. And I played with a bunch of boys out here. One of the boys is a trombone player, he works out there with Waltz Living Studio. You see Ward Kimball, I don't know if you've ever heard of him. Oh yes, the firehouse fire. Well believe it or not, Joe Dantzburg and I started them out. Oh really?
Yes sir, that's really true.

Nothing proved it. I believe it. And now we did, they had a little band, and on a Sunday afternoon after we met them, my wife and all, we used to go out here and he lives in St. Gable. We used to go out there and make a big pot of gumbo and he'd get a big tub of soda water and beer, and we'd jam out there. And we'd start, they were playing but I mean we'd.
Was Johnny Lucas ripping that little iron? Yeah, at that time, yeah. He had no Johnny Lucas at all.
Yeah. Because the, my, the symbol, I have a Chinese symbol that he made me prisoner. An old style Chinese symbol, not a late one. See, you couldn't buy one like I got now. You don't sell them.
No, most of them don't use the Chinese.
No, listen, when I got a couple Chinese, see, an old, old,

original Chinese album, he'd give it to me. And we used to go out there putting it every Sunday afternoon. I'd have a big crowd, this band that kept on playing and playing and playing, and then went out to Walsh, did it in the studio one time, played a couple of times with them. Next thing I heard they'd come up there at Five Plus Two. And every Christmas he sends me a card. When I came back from Europe, they were playing out at Beverly Cavill on Friday nights, so I went out there one Friday night and I didn't think the guy had seen me. I was sitting out with some people, and just before he started playing the number, he said, ladies and gentlemen, I want to introduce you. I said, gentlemen, I think you all know him. In fact, he calls me doing what I'm doing right. Not playing music, but what I'm doing right. That's the way he calls. So Ram Hall is sitting over there. Joe Dance Boy.
I was going to ask about your sticks, the weight of your sticks, if you use heavy or light sticks. I use kind of between, about middle weight.
I can't use quite a heavy stick or two. I use about a 7a. 7a.
You never use brushes very much? Oh yeah. I've heard you do it at the beginning. Yeah.
Some pieces I use them quite a bit, but I can put in there and do as much as my sticks. I can with brushes. I can play that song.
That's what Baby Dog says too. Yeah. I can.

I just don't have to have them. But that's what a lot of people, that's why when I was in Europe, this big rat I was telling you about, he wrote up and says, he don't understand how I could play that song. He said, I must have had match sticks playing. See, the rat if you wrote about it.

But I tried to control them. See, I got that drag roll, you know, we call it a drag roll. About the same as the press roll? Yeah, but I can make them put this out there. I can make sticks and make them sound like wire breasts.

A few years, the tiny thing I had, wire breasts. But at that time, I'd use them some time on certain pieces. In the last three years, I used wire breasts more than I've lived in my life. I already needed them.

Well, I was going to say, did you find that little article about, you might look at that and make a note on here. About the Europe thing? That is about the Europe one, yes. And did you find the other one about when you're in W. Dine? No, no, I can't think of what. Well, we'll look at that.
I think it was in 1936. Now, see this piece here, see, when I was 59 years old.
Oh, yes. That's when you returned to the United States.
That's right. Yeah, when I got sick over that to come back.
Yeah. Well, you're 58 years old. Well, you were in Germany, then you left and came back.

Yeah, I had to come back. They all decided, the band decided that it was best for me to come back home and try to get all right and then rejoin the band again. So they had this meeting. And that's where I was sent back home. Yeah.
And they used Walter Bishop.
Yeah, that's the first night I was off, they used a German boy's drummer.
Oh, yeah.
It was a pretty good drummer. Yeah, I met over in Germany.
Yeah.

And he got more kick out of him than he ever got in his lap, see. So he played a while and then they met this Bishop. And somehow or another, they didn't get along so well with Orie, see, because I tell you, everybody can't play with Orie. No, that's right. He wants you to play like he wants you to play, you know. Well I got used to it, see. I said it doesn't make me no different, you know. But a lot of guys won't do that, see. He's got a certain way he wants you to play. And not all the time, you know. And that's why a lot of fellas can't get along with Orie, see. As far as he's a swell fella, you can't beat him. He just, he likes, he's got that old time rhythm like that. And that's where he wants you to play. And that's what I used to do. Sometimes he'd get over and say, ah, come on, give me that right rhythm, you know. Yeah. Get on that right rhythm, you know. He loves his rhythm. Can't beat him for that.

I was going to ask you the last time you went back to New Orleans, how long ago was that? I think you told us last time. When I left New Orleans? No, when was the last time you went back for a visit? I've never been back. Since 1917? Eighteen. Eighteen. I've never been back. That's what I thought you said, it had been a long time. No, never been. I thought maybe you'd been back though some time.
The closest I've been back to Houston, Texas, when O'Replay for Full of Brits have come at that convention.
Since you first went to Chicago then you haven't been back. I don't know if you'd gone back.

I've been back from here to Chicago, but I left there never been back. That's why I said I was supposed to go back with a band, but we never did go. My brother went back, the first time he went back he went with Louis. Yeah, 1931. That's the first only band Louis made up himself. He made that band up himself. But I had never been back. I left there in 1918, never been back.
Well I think that's about the end of this tape here, unless there's something else you wanted to say, but I think that covers your life pretty well.
Yeah, well, nice talking to you. I certainly enjoyed it.
I know people appreciate hearing this. Yeah. I hope I can get a chance to go back there again. I hope so too. They'd like to see you.
Something might come up there, might be able to go back. Because I've heard many times. stuff

segments.title: How he got the nickname Ram and first sat in with Kid Ory
segments.summary: Hall explains the nickname Kid Ory gave him and how he first played with Ory at St. Catherine Hall, substituting for Ory's drummer Henry Martin.

segments.title: Brother Tubby gives him his first sticks
segments.summary: Tubby, called Baby, handed him a pair of sticks and he began beating on porch steps; this is how he picked up drumming.

segments.title: Born 1897 in Sellers, Louisiana; father Joseph Hall the brass band drummer
segments.summary: Hall gives his birth date and place, the move to New Orleans at about two, and his father's drumming in a country brass band.

segments.title: First job: filling in for Tubby on a Plaquemines Parish engagement
segments.summary: In short pants, borrowing long trousers, he substituted for his brother with a band playing below New Orleans and was hired from then on.

segments.title: Tubby's age and how Fred Hall became Tubby
segments.summary: Tubby was two years older, born around 1895; his real name was Fred Hall and he was nicknamed for being fat, with Minor called Little Tubby.

segments.title: First three-piece band with Arthur Campbell and Sidney Bechet
segments.summary: His first job was upstairs at a nightclub on Gravier Alley in a trio with pianist Arthur Campbell and Sidney Bechet.

segments.title: Following Tubby to Chicago in 1918 and the stockyard job
segments.summary: Tubby and others went to the Deluxe Cafe in Chicago; Hall and his parents were sent for, he walked off a stockyard job and took his brother's place when Tubby was drafted.

segments.title: The Dreamland band and how Oliver took over from Mutt Carey
segments.summary: Hall describes the Dreamland band with Sugar Johnny, Lil Hardin, Mutt Carey and Dodds, and how Oliver took the band while Carey was away in New Orleans.

segments.title: Pekin gangsters, Al Capone and the Royal Garden
segments.summary: Working after hours at the Pekin ended amid shootings and gangsters, where he first saw Al Capone; Oliver then got work at the Royal Garden.

segments.title: San Francisco with Oliver and the dispute that ended it
segments.summary: The band went to San Francisco with Davey Jones added; Hall refused to lay off Jimmy Palao, Oliver dismissed him, the union ruled in his favour, and he returned to Chicago to work with Jimmy Noone.

segments.title: Opening a Chicago club with Jimmy Noone and Earl Hines
segments.summary: Hall opened a club with Noone and Hines, and left after trouble with a married coat-check girl.

segments.title: Moving to Los Angeles: Ory's taxi dance hall band
segments.summary: Ory sent for him to work a Los Angeles taxi dance hall; he lost a vote for the job by one vote but stayed, and became Ory's regular drummer with Mutt Carey, Bud Scott and Eddie Garland.

segments.title: Bad years before the war and being drafted again at 44
segments.summary: Music slumped before the war, Hall worked a five-piece band at Strip City, and was drafted a second time at age 44.

segments.title: Fresno, the Douglas aircraft plant and quitting for a Hollywood club job
segments.summary: Stationed in Fresno, he then took a defense job at Douglas, led a plant band, and left in a tuxedo to open at a Hollywood club, telling his supervisor he was joining the service.

segments.title: Ory's early radio band, Zutty and Ory's temper
segments.summary: Hall recalls Ory's band working for Standard Oil, trouble between Ory and Zutty, and Ory's temper.

segments.chapter: New Orleans memories and early drumming
segments.title: Early music in New Orleans: his ambitions and picnic excursion boats
segments.summary: Hall remembers wanting to play a funeral, a Mardi Gras parade and a picnic, and Ory's riverboat excursion jobs.

segments.chapter: New Orleans memories and early drumming
segments.title: Henry Martin, Joe Lindsey and drummers with Ory in New Orleans
segments.summary: They discuss Ory's earlier drummers, Henry Martin and Joe Lindsey, and Hall says he left New Orleans in 1918 so knows little of later players.

segments.chapter: New Orleans memories and early drumming
segments.title: Tubby Hall's drumming style and visit to Los Angeles
segments.summary: Tubby came to California with a revue, played a different rhythm and had a famous press roll that Baby Dodds reportedly copied.

segments.chapter: New Orleans memories and early drumming
segments.title: What Ory taught him about rhythm
segments.summary: Hall credits Ory with insisting on good plain rhythm rather than fancy playing.

segments.chapter: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
segments.title: His first drum set, bass drum and foot pedal
segments.summary: Hall describes his first outfit with snare, one cymbal, cowbell and wood block, rope-tension bass drums, gut snares and the early wooden pedal.

segments.chapter: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
segments.title: Favorite drummer Chick Webb
segments.summary: Asked which drummers he liked, Hall names Chick Webb as his favorite of all time and says where he heard him.

segments.chapter: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
segments.title: Early New Orleans drummers: Cantrell, Henry Zeno and others
segments.summary: Hall talks about older New Orleans drummers including Cantrell and Henry Zeno and where they played.

segments.chapter: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
segments.title: Living on Forest Street and his Humphrey cousins
segments.summary: He gives his New Orleans address and discusses cousins, the Humphrey family, including Percy and Willie, and their instruments.

segments.chapter: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
segments.title: Walter Brundy, Buddy Bolden and the drummers he never knew
segments.summary: Hall remembers Walter Brundy, doesn't recall other old drummers, and saw Buddy Bolden once at Lincoln Park.

segments.chapter: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
segments.title: Sidney Bechet's age and seeing Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: They compare Bechet's age to Hall's, Hall notes meeting Bechet in Europe in 1957, and recalls first seeing Louis Armstrong in a parade.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, lessons and Tubby's story
segments.title: Brass bands, Mardi Gras and the Elks convention parade
segments.summary: Hall names brass bands he heard, says he played snare in Mardi Gras and funerals but never in a regular brass band, and describes a trip with Mutt Carey's band to the Elks convention.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, lessons and Tubby's story
segments.title: Learning to read music from Jimmy Bertrand in Chicago
segments.summary: Tubby showed him how to hold sticks; he first learned to read notes in Chicago from Jimmy Bertrand.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, lessons and Tubby's story
segments.title: When and why Tubby went to Chicago
segments.summary: They work out that Tubby went north in 1917 before Oliver, and joined the Deluxe Cafe band though he may not have gone to play music.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, lessons and Tubby's story
segments.title: Creole cigar makers and Hall's Creole background
segments.summary: Hall says Tubby had no trade but office work, most Creole men went north as cigar makers, and his father's side was Creole.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, lessons and Tubby's story
segments.title: No relation to Edmund Hall, and Tubby's first Chicago work
segments.summary: Hall clears up that he is not related to Edmund Hall, and says Tubby played small jobs with a doctor's band before joining the Dixieland group.

segments.title: Tig Chambers, Freddie Keppard and the Original Dixieland band
segments.summary: Other New Orleans bands that went north, and how the Original Dixieland band's Livery Stable Blues recording made Dixieland popular.

segments.title: His own records: Decca, Columbia and Good Time Jazz
segments.summary: Hall says he was not on the 1921 Spikes Brothers sides; his first records were for Decca, then Columbia and Good Time Jazz.

segments.title: Playing with Dink Johnson and gigs out west
segments.summary: Allen asks about Dink Johnson; Hall played a few one-nighters with him and says most of his California work was with Mutt Carey and Ory.

segments.chapter: Ory, Mutt and New Orleans life
segments.title: How old Ory and Mutt Carey are
segments.summary: They discuss the argument over Ory's age; Hall puts him around 73 and Mutt a year or two younger.

segments.chapter: Ory, Mutt and New Orleans life
segments.title: Ory's swing beating other bands on the wagons
segments.summary: Hall recalls Ory's band in New Orleans winning street contests with a swinging rhythm, including a time with King Oliver.

segments.chapter: Ory, Mutt and New Orleans life
segments.title: Playing on riverboat picnics and lakefront outings
segments.summary: Hall describes the colored boat rides up the river, playing for the picnic, and playing at Milneburg and West End.

segments.chapter: Ory, Mutt and New Orleans life
segments.title: Church music and religion in New Orleans
segments.summary: Hall went to Baptist church and Sunday school as a child, later became Catholic, and discusses church music and Creole Catholics.

segments.chapter: Ory, Mutt and New Orleans life
segments.title: Bolden, walking to jobs and carrying instruments
segments.summary: He first saw Bolden around age twelve to fifteen and recalls walking long distances with drums, with Eddie Garland carrying his bass.

segments.title: Bud Scott and the rhythm section of Ory's band
segments.summary: Hall met Bud Scott in California, and describes Ory's soft but driving rhythm section and its reception.

segments.title: Four beats versus two beats and Cantrell's tuning advice
segments.summary: Hall says New Orleans drummers always played four beats, and relates the drum-tuning advice from an old drummer named Cantrell.

segments.title: Drum size, tuning the snare and bass drum
segments.summary: Hall and Allen talk about his drums, shell depth and tuning the bass drum to a pitch.

segments.title: Hi-hat, Chinese cymbal and the Firehouse Five Plus Two
segments.summary: Hall describes adopting the hi-hat, his old Chinese cymbal, and his friendship with Ward Kimball and Disney players who jammed at his home.

segments.title: Sticks and brushes
segments.summary: He uses medium-weight 7A sticks, plays brushes when needed, and makes a drag roll that can sound like wire brushes.

segments.title: Illness on the 1957 Europe tour and replacing him with Ory
segments.summary: Hall had to return from Germany ill; the band used other drummers, and he explains that not everyone gets along with Ory's rhythmic demands.

segments.title: Never returning to New Orleans since 1918
segments.summary: Hall has not been back to New Orleans since leaving in 1918, and notes Tubby went back with Louis in 1931.

segments.title: Closing of the interview
segments.summary: The tape ends with thanks and hopes of a future visit.
